title: Pure-nature man would be as ignorant and weak as fallen man, and outwardly worse off, lacking Adam's tradition and the promise of Christ
source_text: XXI. Ac proinde quantum ad internas animi vires, tantam in pura natura futuram ignorantiam, beneque cogitandi, judicandi, & vivendi infirmitatem, peccandique pronitatem, quantam in natura lapsa experimur. Quantum ad externa vero majorem. Nam praeterquam quod objecta sensibilia concupiscentiam excitantia essent eadem, mala pravorum hominum consilia, & exempla potentius tunc ad malum provocarent. Nam cognitio Dei virtutumque quae Adamo communicata fuerat, & memoria promissionum & comminationum Dei, priorisque status & praeteriti lapsus recordatio, & promissio venturi Christi, cum spe redemptionis ejus, quae per traditionem a capite in posteros diffusa promanarunt; peccandi facilitatem in natura lapsa mitigare potuerunt, ut hac in parte caecitas, corruptio morum generalior, peccandique pronitas in pura natura proclivior futura fuisse videatur.
pass_a_gloss: And therefore as regards the inner powers of the soul, there would be as much ignorance in pure nature, and weakness of thinking, judging, and living well, and proneness to sinning, as we experience in fallen nature. But as regards external things, more. For besides that the sensible objects exciting concupiscence would be the same, the bad counsels and examples of wicked men would then provoke to evil more powerfully. For the knowledge of God and of the virtues which had been communicated to Adam, and the memory of God's promises and threats, and the remembrance of the former state and the past fall, and the promise of the coming Christ, with the hope of his redemption, which flowed by tradition from the head to the descendants; could mitigate the facility of sinning in fallen nature, so that in this part blindness, a more general corruption of morals, and proneness to sinning would seem likely to have been more inclined in pure nature.
pass_b_english: So with regard to the inner powers of the soul, there would be as much ignorance in pure nature, as much weakness in thinking, judging and living well, and as much proneness to sin, as we experience in fallen nature. With regard to outward things there would be more.

The sense objects that stir up desire would be the same, and besides that, the evil counsel and example of wicked men would then urge men to evil more strongly. For in fallen nature the ease of sinning could be softened by what had come down by tradition from the head of the race to his descendants: the knowledge of God and of the virtues that had been given to Adam, the memory of God's promises and threats, the recollection of the former state and of the fall, and the promise of the coming Christ with the hope of his redemption.
So on this score blindness, a more widespread corruption of morals, and the tendency to sin would apparently have been greater in pure nature.

lemmas.gloss: from the head of the race to his descendants

choices.english: the promise of the coming Christ
choices.why: Le Blanc means the first gospel promise handed down from Adam; 'the coming Christ' keeps the forward look.
